title: The Prophets close
hook: the Talmud says after the prophets, prophecy passed to the wise, and to children and fools (Bava Batra 12b)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malachi's last promise: Elijah turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other. Your line was turn the hearts. What did you ask across a generation, and what did you hear? Today, the prophets go quiet. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

Malachi rolls up, and the section of the Bible called the Prophets is done. This year opened it the day Moses died, with Joshua told to be strong. Since then: judges and kings, and prophets who argued, wept and waited, and the Twelve, from Hosea's broken marriage to Malachi's turning hearts. And then silence. The rabbis felt that silence, and they asked a question about it. When the prophets stop, where does the voice go? Their answer, in the Talmud's tractate Bava Batra, has a surprise at the end.
screen: `MALACHI ROLLS UP.` → `JOSHUA TO MALACHI.` → `WHERE DOES THE VOICE GO?`

segments.voice: Here is the passage, retold. Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa teaches: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to the wise. The Talmud pushes back right away: isn't a sage a prophet too? It answers that prophecy was taken from the prophets, but not from the wise. Then a teacher named Amemar adds: the sage is greater than the prophet. That's a bold thing to say, and it tells you how the rabbis saw their own work. The voice didn't vanish. It moved into study: into people sitting with these very books, arguing over a verse, asking what it asks of us now. Every one of these days, from Micah's three verbs to Habakkuk's one line, has been that kind of listening. Then comes the surprise. Rabbi Yochanan says: from the day the Temple was destroyed, prophecy was taken from the prophets and given to fools and to children. The Talmud even tells a story of a passing remark, from someone nobody took seriously, that turned out to be true. Readers have heard this in more than one way. Some hear a joke with an edge: these days, prophecy is so cheapened that only fools speak it. Others hear something tender: the truth now turns up where nobody guards it. A child says the thing every adult in the room was too careful to say. A stranger's offhand line answers the question you've carried for a month. Both readings agree on this much. The prophets close, but listening doesn't. The scrolls are finished. The people reading them, arguing over them, and sometimes hearing a true word from the least likely mouth in the room, are not.
screen: `GIVEN TO THE WISE.` · `THE SAGE IS GREATER THAN THE PROPHET.` · then, large: `GIVEN TO FOOLS AND TO CHILDREN.` · then: `THE PROPHETS CLOSE, LISTENING DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: For today's practice, listen for wisdom from a child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something a child once said that stopped you. A question you couldn't answer. A blunt truth at the dinner table. A small kindness they didn't know was big. If no child comes to mind, think of someone you don't usually listen to, and something they said that turned out right. Hold their words for a while. Then just listen to the room around you, the small sounds nobody guards, for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can let the listening be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bava Batra, the Talmud tractate where the rabbis say that when the Prophets closed, their voice passed to the wise, and to fools and children. Today's word.
Your line: the voice goes on. Today, listen to one child, or one person you usually talk over, all the way to the end of their sentence. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Jews read from the Prophets in synagogue on Shabbat and festivals as the haftarah, and the Talmud's discussion of where prophecy went is studied as part of the tradition's own account of rabbinic learning.

fork.setup: you're a rabbi after the Temple fell. the prophets are silent. where do you say the voice went?
options: to the wise, and to fools and children.
fork.reveal: Bava Batra says prophecy was given to the wise, and Rabbi Yochanan adds: to fools and to children.

original.note: Hebrew: "prophets," the name of the section of the Bible that closes with Malachi.

trapdoor: what you thought: when the prophets stopped, God went quiet.
what it means: the rabbis say the voice moved, into study, and into the mouths of children.
what a scholar hears: Bava Batra's two teachings side by side, the sage greater than the prophet, and prophecy given to fools and children.

notes: Editor pass: hook list no longer repeats day 831's coal and dry bones; Bava Batra 12a retold more exactly (the Gemara's answer, then Amemar's 'the sage is greater'); 'each Shabbat' softened; varied the practice opener.
The look-back names the year's opening (day 697, the Prophets begin the day Moses dies; day 698, Joshua 1). No day counts stated.

Bava Batra 12a–b paraphrased: Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa (prophecy given to the wise); 'a sage is greater than a prophet' (Amemar); Rabbi Yochanan (given to fools and children); the story of the fool's remark (Mar bar Rav Ashi). Keeper please confirm attributions.
The two readings of Rabbi Yochanan (ironic vs tender) are offered as 'some hear', unranked; confirm.
Audit pass: cut the end-of-teach look-back list of carries, which repeated day 833's week-end look-back almost line for line; replaced with a close on the passage itself.

Bava Batra 12a dates the change 'from the day the Temple was destroyed' (usually read as the First Temple), while Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi prophesied after it; the script does not say which Temple. Keeper may want a line on that tension.
